title: Das Lämmchen und Fischchen
titleEn: The Little Lamb and the Little Fish
part: The Little Lamb and the Little Fish
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 141. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (todt, gieng, fiengen, thate).
about: KHM 141 retells the transformation-and-rescue pattern familiar from "Little Brother and Little Sister" in miniature: a brother and sister, tormented by their witch-stepmother, are cursed mid-song into a fish and a lamb after a children's game goes wrong, and a passing bride recognizes the lamb's grief in its bleating. The tale's heart is the repeated singsong rhyme the children chant while playing, which comes back transformed once the curse falls, so the sound of the words does real narrative work.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Brüderchen und Schwesterchen, die hatten sich herzlich lieb.
sentences.l: There was once a little-brother and little-sister, they had each other heartily dear.
sentences.i: There were once a little brother and a little sister who loved each other dearly.
sentences.n: “sich lieb haben” — to hold one another dear — is the ordinary German for loving each other. “die hatten sich…” takes the pair up again with a demonstrative, a spoken turn the tales use constantly.

sentences.t: Ihre rechte Mutter war aber todt, und sie hatten eine Stiefmutter, die war ihnen nicht gut und that ihnen heimlich alles Leid an.
sentences.l: Their right mother was however dead, and they had a stepmother, she was to them not good and did to them secretly every harm.
sentences.i: But their true mother was dead, and they had a stepmother who was not good to them and secretly did them every harm.
sentences.n: “recht” here means true, proper — the real mother, not the step one. “todt” is the 1857 spelling of tot. “Leid antun”, to do someone harm, is separable and the halves stand apart: “that … an” (thun and that are the 1857 forms of tun and tat).

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß die zwei mit andern Kindern auf einer Wiese vor dem Haus spielten,
sentences.l: It carried itself to that the two with other children on a meadow before the house played,
sentences.i: It came to pass that the two were playing with other children on a meadow in front of the house,
sentences.n: “sich zutragen” — to come to pass — is reflexive and separable: “es trug sich zu”. It opens episodes all through the tales.

sentences.t: und an der Wiese war ein Teich, der gieng bis an die eine Seite vom Haus.
sentences.l: and at the meadow was a pond, that went up to the one side of the house.
sentences.i: and beside the meadow was a pond that reached right up to one side of the house.
sentences.n: “der” opening the second clause is a demonstrative — and that one went… The pond touching the house is what later lets the fish follow the lamb indoors.

sentences.t: Die Kinder liefen da herum, kriegten sich und spielten Abzählens:
sentences.l: The children ran about there, caught each other and played counting-out:
sentences.i: The children ran about there, caught one another, and played at counting-out:
sentences.n: “kriegten sich” is catching one another at play; kriegen in its everyday sense is to get, to receive. “Abzählens” is an old adverbial genitive — to play at counting-out: the rhyme that follows decides who must run.

sentences.t:
„Eneke, Beneke, lat mi liewen,
will die ock min Vügelken giewen.
Vügelken sall mie Strau söken,
Strau will ick den Köseken giewen,
Köseken sall mie Melk giewen,
Melk will ick den Bäcker giewen,
Bäcker sall mie ’n Kocken backen,
Kocken will ick den Kätken giewen,
Kätken sall mie Müse fangen,
Müse will ick in ’n Rauck hangen
un will se anschnien.“
sentences.l:
“Eneke, Beneke, let me live,
[then] will [I] to you also my little-bird give.
Little-bird shall for me straw seek,
straw will I to the little-cow give,
little-cow shall for me milk give,
milk will I to the baker give,
baker shall for me a cake bake,
cake will I to the little-cat give,
little-cat shall for me mice catch,
mice will I in the smoke hang
and will them cut up.”
sentences.i:
“Eneke, Beneke, let me live,
and I will give you my little bird as well.
The little bird shall seek me straw,
the straw I will give to the little cow,
the little cow shall give me milk,
the milk I will give to the baker,
the baker shall bake me a cake,
the cake I will give to the little cat,
the little cat shall catch me mice,
the mice I will hang up in the smoke
and cut them up.”
sentences.n: A counting-out rhyme in Low German (Westphalian), printed in dialect inside an otherwise High German tale: “lat” = laß, “mi” = mich, “mie” = mir, “die” = dir (not the article here), “ick” = ich, “min” = mein, “ock” = auch, “sall” = soll, “giewen” = geben, “söken” = suchen, “un” = und, “se” = sie. “’n” is the elided article, einen or den. The chain runs bird → straw → cow → milk → baker → cake → cat → mice, each link paying for the next, and the German rhymes “liewen” with “giewen” at the opening and “fangen” with “hangen” near the close, the middle lines chiming instead on the repeated “giewen”; the idiomatic lines here do not rhyme. The second line has neither a subject nor a “dann” of its own, so “[then]” and “[I]” are supplied in square brackets to let the English stand. The last word, “anschnien” (anschneiden, to cut into), is the word that decides who must run.

sentences.t: Dabei standen sie in einem Kreiß, und auf welchen nun das Wort „anschnien“ fiel, der mußte fortlaufen, und die anderen liefen ihm nach und fiengen ihn.
sentences.l: In doing it stood they in a ring, and upon whom now the word “anschnien” fell, he had to run away, and the others ran after him and caught him.
sentences.i: As they said it they stood in a ring, and whoever the word “anschnien” fell upon had to run away, and the others ran after him and caught him.
sentences.n: “auf welchen … der …” puts the clause first and takes it up again with “der”: whoever it fell on, he had to run. “fiengen” here is fangen, caught — not anfangen, began; the 1857 spelling serves both verbs. “Kreiß” is the 1857 spelling of Kreis.

sentences.t: Wie sie so fröhlich dahinsprangen, sah’s die Stiefmutter vom Fenster mit an und ärgerte sich.
sentences.l: As they so merrily leapt along, saw it the stepmother from the window on and vexed herself.
sentences.i: As they were leaping merrily about, the stepmother looked on from the window and was vexed.
sentences.n: “mit ansehen”, to look on at a thing, is separable and its halves stand far apart: “sah’s … mit an”. “sah’s” = sah es. “sich ärgern” is reflexive where English has a plain verb.

sentences.t: Weil sie aber Hexenkünste verstand, so verwünschte sie beide, das Brüderchen in einen Fisch und das Schwesterchen in ein Lamm.
sentences.l: Because she however witch-arts understood, so cursed she both, the little-brother into a fish and the little-sister into a lamb.
sentences.i: But because she knew the arts of witchcraft, she laid a spell on them both — the little brother into a fish and the little sister into a lamb.
sentences.n: “verstehen” with an object means to know a thing, to have the skill of it. “verwünschen” is to curse in the sense of transforming by a spell, and it is the tales’ standard word for enchantment. A weil-clause answered by “so” is the older word order.

sentences.t: Da schwamm das Fischchen im Teich hin und her, und war traurig,
sentences.l: There swam the little-fish in the pond back and forth, and was sad,
sentences.i: So the little fish swam back and forth in the pond, and was sad,
sentences.n: “hin und her” — this way and that. The diminutives Fischchen and Lämmchen keep the children present inside the animals; the tale calls them nothing else from here on.

sentences.t: das Lämmchen gieng auf der Wiese hin und her, und war traurig und fraß nicht und rührte kein Hälmchen an.
sentences.l: the little-lamb went on the meadow back and forth, and was sad and ate not and touched not a little-blade.
sentences.i: the little lamb went back and forth on the meadow, and was sad, and would not eat, and did not touch a single blade of grass.
sentences.n: “fressen” is the verb used of animals eating, and it fits the lamb while sounding harsher than essen. “anrühren” is separable: “rührte … an”.

sentences.t: So gieng eine lange Zeit hin, da kamen fremde Gäste auf das Schloß.
sentences.l: So went a long time by, then came strange guests to the castle.
sentences.i: So a long time went by, and then strangers came as guests to the castle.
sentences.n: “hingehen” of time means to pass: “gieng … hin”. “fremd” is unknown, from elsewhere — visitors, not enemies. The castle appears here for the first time: the children belong to the house.

sentences.t: Die falsche Stiefmutter dachte „jetzt ist die Gelegenheit gut,“
sentences.l: The false stepmother thought “now is the opportunity good,”
sentences.i: The treacherous stepmother thought, “Now the chance is a good one,”
sentences.n: “falsch” of a person means treacherous, two-faced — not mistaken. The thought is given in direct speech, exactly as speech aloud would be.

sentences.t: rief den Koch, und sprach zu ihm „geh und hol das Lamm von der Wiese und schlachts, wir haben sonst nichts für die Gäste.“
sentences.l: called the cook, and spoke to him “go and fetch the lamb from the meadow and slaughter it, we have otherwise nothing for the guests.”
sentences.i: called the cook and said to him, “Go and fetch the lamb from the meadow and slaughter it — we have nothing else for the guests.”
sentences.n: “der Koch” is the cook; the bare form koch is also the imperative of kochen, which is not what stands here. “schlachts” = schlachte es, the pronoun swallowed into the imperative, like “sah’s” above.

sentences.t: Da gieng der Koch hin und holte das Lämmchen und führte es in die Küche und band ihm die Füßchen;
sentences.l: There went the cook off and fetched the little-lamb and led it into the kitchen and bound to it the little-feet;
sentences.i: So the cook went off and fetched the little lamb and led it into the kitchen and tied its little feet;
sentences.n: “band” is the past of binden, to tie — not the noun das Band. Dative of possession: “band ihm die Füßchen”, tied the feet on it, where English says its feet. Four clauses on und: the sentence moves at the speed of the deed.

sentences.t: das litt es alles geduldig.
sentences.l: that suffered it all patiently.
sentences.i: and it bore all of that patiently.
sentences.n: “leiden” here is to put up with, to let happen. “es” is the lamb: das Lämmchen is neuter, and so the sister inside it is ‘it’ throughout.

sentences.t: Wie er nun sein Messer herausgezogen hatte und auf der Schwelle wetzte, um es abzustechen, sah es, wie ein Fischlein in dem Wasser vor dem Gossenstein hin und her schwamm und zu ihm hinaufblickte.
sentences.l: As he now his knife drawn out had and on the threshold whetted, in order it to stick, saw it how a little-fish in the water before the drain-stone back and forth swam and up to it looked.
sentences.i: Now when he had drawn his knife and was whetting it on the threshold, in order to stick the lamb, the lamb saw a little fish swimming back and forth in the water in front of the drain-stone and looking up at it.
sentences.n: The subject of “sah” is still the lamb, “es”; German lets the pronoun stand where English has to name the creature again. “abstechen” is the butcher’s word — to kill by driving the knife in. “der Gossenstein” is the stone slab of the kitchen drain, where the water ran out of the house, which is how the fish can be there at all.

sentences.t: Das war aber das Brüderchen, denn als das Fischchen gesehen hatte wie der Koch das Lämmchen fortführte, war es im Teich mitgeschwommen bis zum Haus.
sentences.l: That was however the little-brother, for when the little-fish seen had how the cook the little-lamb led away, had it in the pond along-swum up to the house.
sentences.i: But that was the little brother: when the little fish had seen the cook leading the little lamb away, it had swum along in the pond as far as the house.
sentences.n: “mitschwimmen”, to swim along with, is separable and stands here in the past perfect with sein — “war … mitgeschwommen”. German verbs of motion take sein, not haben, in the perfect.

sentences.t: Da rief das Lämmchen hinab
sentences.l: Then called the little-lamb down
sentences.i: Then the little lamb called down
sentences.n: “hinabrufen”, to call down, is separable. The sentence is left open — no colon, no comma: the verse simply follows.

sentences.t:
„ach Brüderchen im tiefen See,
wie thut mir doch mein Herz so weh!
der Koch der wetzt das Messer,
will mir mein Herz durchstechen.“
sentences.l:
“ah little-brother in the deep lake,
how does to me yet my heart so ache!
the cook, he whets the knife,
[he] wants to me my heart to pierce through.”
sentences.i:
“Ah, little brother, down in the deep water,
how my heart aches!
The cook is whetting the knife,
he means to pierce my heart through.”
sentences.n: The German rhymes See / weh, and the idiomatic line does not attempt to rhyme. “thut … weh” is wehtun, to hurt, split around the pronoun; “doch” presses the cry home and has no single English word. “der Koch der wetzt” repeats the subject as a pronoun, a spoken pattern. The subject of the last line is gapped, and [he] is supplied. “im tiefen See” has See masculine, the lake; the fish’s answering verse has it feminine, die See, the sea — the gender bends to the verse.

sentences.t: Das Fischchen antwortete
sentences.l: The little-fish answered
sentences.n: Again no colon: the 1857 text lets the answer stand as its own block of verse, with nothing but the speech tag before it.

sentences.t:
„ach Schwesterchen in der Höh,
wie thut mir doch mein Herz so weh
in dieser tiefen See!“
sentences.l:
“ah little-sister up on the height,
how does to me yet my heart so ache
in this deep sea!”
sentences.i:
“Ah, little sister, up above,
how my heart aches
down in this deep water!”
sentences.n: The answer echoes the call line for line, setting “Höh” — Höhe, the height, up above — against the deep: the fish below, the lamb above. The rhyme is Höh / weh. Here “See” is feminine, “dieser tiefen See”, where the lamb’s verse had it masculine; both genders exist in German, der See a lake and die See the sea.

sentences.t: Wie der Koch hörte daß das Lämmchen sprechen konnte und so traurige Worte zu dem Fischchen hinabrief, erschrack er und dachte es müßte kein natürliches Lämmchen sein, sondern wäre von der bösen Frau im Haus verwünscht.
sentences.l: As the cook heard that the little-lamb speak could and such sad words to the little-fish down called, took fright he and thought it must be no natural little-lamb, but rather were by the wicked woman in the house enchanted.
sentences.i: When the cook heard that the little lamb could speak and called such sad words down to the little fish, he took fright and thought it could be no natural lamb, but must be under a spell laid by the wicked woman in the house.
sentences.n: “erschrack” is the 1857 spelling of erschrak. From “es müßte” onward the German goes into the subjunctive of reported thought — müßte, wäre — which marks all of it as what the cook thought, not what the tale asserts.

sentences.t: Da sprach er „sei ruhig, ich will dich nicht schlachten“
sentences.l: Then spoke he “be still, I will you not slaughter”
sentences.i: Then he said, “Be still, I will not slaughter you,”
sentences.n: “sei” is the imperative of sein. The closing quotation mark is followed by no comma at all and the sentence runs straight on into the next verb — 1857 punctuation of speech is lighter than ours.

sentences.t: nahm ein anderes Thier und bereitete das für die Gäste,
sentences.l: took an other animal and prepared that for the guests,
sentences.i: took another beast and prepared that for the guests,
sentences.n: “Thier” is the 1857 spelling of Tier. The tale does not soften what this means: something else is killed in the lamb’s place.

sentences.t: und brachte das Lämmchen zu einer guten Bäuerin, der erzählte er alles, was er gesehen und gehört hatte.
sentences.l: and brought the little-lamb to a good farmer’s-wife, to her told he everything that he seen and heard had.
sentences.i: and brought the little lamb to a good farmer’s wife, and told her everything he had seen and heard.
sentences.n: “der” here is the dative of die — to her — set first to hook the clause onto the woman just named; German links sentences this way where English would begin a new one.

sentences.t: Die Bäuerin war aber gerade die Amme von dem Schwesterchen gewesen, vermuthete gleich wer’s sein würde und gieng mit ihm zu einer weisen Frau.
sentences.l: The farmer’s-wife had however just the nurse of the little-sister been, guessed at once who it would be and went with it to a wise woman.
sentences.i: But the farmer’s wife had been the little sister’s own nurse, and guessed at once who it must be, and went with the lamb to a wise woman.
sentences.n: “gerade” here means precisely, none other than. “vermuthete” is the 1857 spelling of vermutete, and “wer’s” = wer es. “eine weise Frau” is the village wise woman, a healer and knower of charms — the counter-figure to the witch in the house.

sentences.t: Da sprach die weise Frau einen Segen über das Lämmchen und Fischchen, wovon sie ihre menschliche Gestalt wieder bekamen,
sentences.l: Then spoke the wise woman a blessing over the little-lamb and little-fish, whereby they their human form again received,
sentences.i: Then the wise woman spoke a blessing over the little lamb and the little fish, by which they got their human form back again,
sentences.n: “einen Segen sprechen” — to speak a blessing — undoes the stepmother’s spell: a word set against a word. “wovon” = whereby, from which.

sentences.t: und danach führte sie beide in einen großen Wald in ein klein Häuschen, wo sie einsam, aber zufrieden und glücklich lebten.
sentences.l: and after that led she both into a great forest into a little house, where they solitary, but content and happy lived.
sentences.i: and after that she led them both into a great forest, into a little house, where they lived alone, but content and happy.
sentences.n: “klein Häuschen” leaves the adjective uninflected, an older usage. “einsam” is alone, apart from others, not lonely — the tale ends with the two of them out of the stepmother’s reach, and never says what became of her.

glossary.band: binden — to tie, bind (3rd sg. past; also das Band, a ribbon or hoop)
glossary.fiengen: fangen — to catch (3rd pl. past; 1857 spelling of fingen; the same form also serves anfangen, to begin)
glossary.koch: der Koch — cook (noun; koch is also the imperative of kochen, to cook)
glossary.kriegten: kriegen — to catch, get hold of (3rd pl. past; also to get, to receive)
glossary.melk: Low German: die Milch — milk (noun; melk is also melken, to milk)
glossary.n: ’n — the elided article, einen or den (Low German: ’n Kocken = einen Kuchen, in ’n Rauck = in den Rauch)
glossary.see: der See — lake (masculine); die See — the sea (feminine)
glossary.weh: weh — sore, painful (weh thun, modern wehtun: to hurt; also das Weh, woe)
glossary.weise: weise — wise (adjective; die weise Frau: the wise woman, the village healer and knower of charms)
glossary.welchen: welcher — which one, whom (here accusative sg. masc.: auf welchen … fiel, on whichever one it fell)
